grammar.title: Narrative tenses
grammar.short: Past simple, past continuous and past perfect

slides.sub: Teen spirit: stories from different generations
slides.hook: Think of the first time you hung out with your friends without your parents. What happened? What was going on? What had you planned before?

rows: Main events of the story, one after another
An action BEFORE another past action

p: Use the past simple for the main actions of your story, in the order they happened.
ex: My friends **showed up** at eight, we **hung out** in the park and we **ended up** at Leo's house.
My grandad **stood up for** a classmate when the teacher was unfair.
Last Saturday I **asked** my cousins **over** to watch a film.

p: Use the past continuous to set the scene, or for a longer action interrupted by a shorter one in the past simple.
ex: Everybody **was hanging out** in the square and music **was playing**.
We **were getting together** for a party when my dad **told** us **off** for the noise.
While my sister **was meeting up with** her friends, I **stayed** at home.

slides.h: Past perfect: one step further back
p: Use the past perfect when you are already in the past and you want to go back to an earlier moment.
ex: When I arrived, my friends **had** already **brought over** the snacks.
Grandma was surprised because she **had never seen** a teenager so addicted to a phone.
I **'d asked** Sara over, but she didn't come along.

rows: When I got home, my parents told me off.
I got home → then they told me off
When I got home, my parents were telling my brother off.
They started before; it was in progress
When I got home, my parents had told my brother off.
It was finished before I arrived

slides.title: The party that went wrong
text: Last summer I **asked** my friends **over** for a party. My parents **had gone** out for the evening, so we **had** the house to ourselves.
We **were dancing** and everyone **was singing** when the doorbell **rang**. It was my neighbour! She **told** us **off** because we **had woken up** her baby.
In the end, we **said** sorry and we **ended up** helping her with the shopping the next day. I think we showed some respect!

items: When I showed up, the party already finished.
When I showed up, the party had already finished.
The party finished before you arrived.
I was knowing it was unfair.
State verbs (know, like, want) don't use continuous forms.
While we hung out at the park, it started to rain.
While we were hanging out at the park, it started to rain.
The longer background action needs the past continuous.

slides.q: By the time we got to the concert, the band ___ on stage.
slides.e: The band appeared before we arrived → past perfect.

slides.q: I ___ with my friends in town when my mum phoned me.
slides.e: Hanging out is the background action interrupted by the phone call.

p: Past continuous = what was happening (the scene).
Past perfect = what had happened before.
Key words: when, while, as, already, by the time, before, after.

slides.sub: Teen spirit: how life was different for other generations
slides.hook: What did your parents use to do at weekends when they were teenagers? Were they dependent on technology?

p: Use 'used to' for past habits and past states that are not true now.
ex: My parents' generation **used to** write letters to their friends.
Teenagers **didn't use to** be so dependent on technology.
**Did** your grandparents **use to** hang out in the town square?

rows: My mum used to have very strong values about manners.
We didn't use to get together online.
Did young people use to respect authority more?
slides.note: In negatives and questions it's 'use to' (no -d).

p: Use 'would' for repeated actions (habits) in the past. It is common when people tell their memories.
Don't use 'would' for past states (be, have, live, like, know).
ex: Every Saturday my grandad **would meet up with** his friends at the café.
My aunt **would** always **bring over** a cake when she visited us.

rows: ✓ We used to hang out at the youth club.
✓ We would hang out at the youth club.
✓ Teachers used to have more authority.

slides.title: Grandma remembers
text: 'When I was sixteen, we **didn't use to** have phones. If you wanted to see your friends, you **would** just go to the square and wait until they **showed up**.
My parents **used to** be very strict. They **would tell** me **off** if I came home late, but I think it was unfair!
We **used to** respect our teachers a lot. Today's generation is different, but I don't judge them. They have strong values too.'

items: My grandparents didn't used to judge people.
My grandparents didn't use to judge people.
Teachers used to have more authority.
'have' is a state here, so 'would' is not possible.
I'm used to hang out at the park as a child.
I used to hang out at the park as a child.
'be used to' means 'be accustomed to' – a different structure.

slides.q: Teenagers in the 1960s ___ be less dependent on technology.
slides.e: 'be' is a state, so only 'used to' is correct.

slides.q: ___ your parents use to get told off at school?
slides.e: Questions with used to: Did + subject + use to...?

p: used to = past habits AND past states.
didn't use to / Did ... use to? (no -d).
For one action at one time, use the past simple.
